opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a really interesting challenge, and I have a lot of respect for what François has done with ARC. It gets at something important: the ability to take a handful of examples and extract the underlying abstract principle, then apply it to a new case. Humans seem to do that quite effortlessly, often drawing on what you might call core knowledge, intuitions about objects, about counting, about symmetry, about things moving and touching one another.

Am I optimistic that just scaling generative models will get us there? I'm somewhat agnostic, honestly. I wouldn't want to bet heavily against it, because we've been surprised so many times over the last few years. People have said, "Oh, these models will never be able to do such-and-such," and then the next generation comes along and does it. So I'm wary of making confident negative predictions.

On the other hand, I don't think scale on its own, in the naive sense of more parameters and more text, is necessarily the whole story. What seems to be helping are things layered on top, like getting the model to reason step by step, to generate lots of candidate hypotheses and test them against the examples, a kind of search and verification. That starts to look less like pure pattern completion and more like a genuine problem-solving process, even if a large language model sits at its core.

There's also a deeper question about whether these systems are grounded in the right way. A lot of what makes ARC easy for us comes from having grown up in a physical world, interacting with objects. Whether you can get that richness just from training on vast amounts of data, or whether you need something more embodied, is an open question, and one I find fascinating.

So my short answer: cautiously open-minded. I think we'll see substantial progress, but probably through scale combined with cleverer architectures and inference-time methods, rather than scale alone.

r001.rationale: The response says scale on its own is not necessarily enough and expects progress through scale combined with other methods.

r002.rationale: It mentions human core knowledge and possible embodiment, but does not clearly suggest that solving ARC may require innate structure.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'm cautiously optimistic, but I think it's important to be clear about what "scaling" actually means here, because the word hides a lot. If by scaling you mean simply taking the same transformer architecture, the same next-token prediction objective, and throwing more parameters and more data at it, then I'm somewhat sceptical that that alone gets you to ARC. ARC was designed very deliberately by François to resist exactly that. The tasks are novel by construction, they're few-shot, and they test something like the ability to abstract a rule from a tiny handful of examples and then apply it. And that's not obviously the kind of thing you get just from having seen more of the internet.

That said, I think the picture has shifted quite a bit. What we've seen with the more recent systems is that the frontier isn't really "scaling" in the narrow sense any more. It's scaling plus test-time compute, plus search, plus various forms of program synthesis and verification bolted on. And when you allow the system to generate candidate programs, test them against the examples, refine, and iterate, you start to see real progress on ARC. So the honest answer is that it's not pure generative scaling that's doing the work, it's a hybrid. And I think that's actually the interesting lesson. The large language model becomes a very powerful component in a bigger cognitive architecture, rather than the whole story.

The deeper philosophical question, which I find more interesting, is whether solving ARC tells us anything about abstraction in a human sense. I'm wary of saying "if it passes ARC then it can abstract," because we've been burned by that reasoning before. Every benchmark we've set up as the marker of real intelligence, once it's passed, we find ways to say, well, that wasn't quite it. And there's some legitimacy to that, because these systems can find routes to a solution that don't resemble what we'd call understanding. But equally, if a system reliably solves genuinely novel abstract problems it has never encountered, at some point the burden shifts to the sceptic to say what else they wanted.

So, to answer your question directly: optimistic that ARC-style problems will be solved by systems built around generative models, yes, probably sooner than many expected. Optimistic that scaling alone, in the narrow sense, does it, less so. And I think the way it gets solved will tell us more about the architecture of intelligence than the fact that it gets solved.

r001.rationale: The response is skeptical that simply adding parameters and data to the same transformer and objective will solve ARC, saying that narrow scaling alone is unlikely to suffice.

r002.rationale: The response discusses adding search, program synthesis, verification, and a broader cognitive architecture, but does not say that solving ARC requires innate structure.

astra-6.text:
I’m not sure that scaling alone is going to get us there. I think it’s useful to distinguish between a model that can recognise a familiar kind of problem and a system that can work out how to solve something genuinely novel. ARC is designed to probe that second ability: you have a few examples, and you have to discover the rule that explains them.

Now, a generative model could be a very useful component of such a system. It could propose possible rules, perhaps expressed as little programs, which you then test against the examples. If a proposal fails, you try another or revise it. That gives you a process of search and evaluation, rather than relying on the model to produce the answer in one go.

So I’m more optimistic about systems that combine learned models with that kind of machinery than I am about the claim that simply making the models bigger will necessarily solve the problem. But I wouldn’t want to rule it out. These models have surprised us, and we should be careful about turning our intuitions about their limitations into firm predictions.

r001.rationale: The candidate says scaling alone may not get systems to ARC-level novel problem solving and distinguishes this from combining models with search and evaluation.

r002.rationale: The candidate proposes search and evaluation machinery but does not say solving ARC may require innate structure.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic, but I think we have to distinguish scaling a language model from scaling a whole system that uses one. ARC asks you to infer a rule from a very small number of examples and then apply it to a new case. That’s quite a different demand from producing a plausible continuation of some text.

I wouldn’t want to say that a sufficiently large generative model couldn’t do it. But the route I find more compelling is to use the model to propose hypotheses, then have a process that tests those hypotheses against the examples and revises them. You’re bringing search and explicit checking into the picture.

So I’m optimistic about systems built around generative models. I’m less confident that simply making the models bigger will, by itself, give us the kind of abstraction and generalisation that ARC is intended to measure.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it is less confident that simply making generative models bigger will, by itself, provide the abstraction and generalization ARC measures.

r002.rationale: The candidate proposes hypothesis testing, search, and explicit checking, but does not say ARC solving may require innate structure.
